1:
Delitzsch sets the psalm beside the Hallel piece before it as the historical member of the group, the festival psalm of the eighth Passover day, built of four tetrastichs that pass by with the swiftness of a bird, as it were with four flappings of its wings; the church sings it, he adds, in a tonus peregrinus distinct from the eight psalm-tones. Clarke finds the poem less settled than that. It carries no title; it reads like a fragment, or part of another psalm, beginning and ending very abruptly, and in many manuscripts and all the versions but one it merely opens the psalm that follows. Authorship has been assigned variously to the three companions of the furnace, to Esther, and to Mordecai. He adds a dating argument drawn from the second verse: the distinction between Israel and Judah arose only after the tribes divided, so the composition must be later than David. Calvin entertains no such questions and takes the whole as a short account of the deliverance, given so that the seed of Abraham might yield themselves wholly to God.

Spurgeon hears the opening as a burst, the poetic fury overleaping all bounds; a soul filled with divine glory cannot fashion a preface but springs at once into the middle of its theme. The emphasis, he says, falls on the coming out — out of the population among whom they had been scattered, out from under the yoke and from the personal grasp of the king who had made them national slaves. They had gone down as a single household and remained one, so united that nobody stayed behind; such unanimity is a pleasing token of the divine presence. Gill presses the same word: they went publicly, not by stealth, and freely, neither forced nor driven, leaving rich and in health, not one feeble among them. Henry has them march out with all the marks of honour rather than steal away.

On the strange speech the voices converge and then diverge. Delitzsch derives the Hebrew term from a root for stammering, and notes that the Greek and the Targum alike render it barbarous. Ellicott judges that translation right, since the word carries the scorn ancient races kept for anyone speaking otherwise, and observes that Russians to this day call Germans dumb. Clarke allows that the phrase may mean nothing beyond a foreign people, though the difference of tongue was real, and records that his old Psalter took it of religion instead, reading the house of Jacob as leaving heathen folk. Henry turns it to a moral: Israel kept their own speech pure and cared nothing for learning their oppressors', and by that separateness preserved an earnest of rescue. Spurgeon adds that the language of foreign taskmasters is never musical in an exile's ear.

Whether Judah in the second verse names one tribe or the nation divides them. Gill rejects both the narrow reading and the architectural one: no tabernacle existed at the exodus, so the word cannot mean a building, and the sense is that the whole body was holiness to the Lord, separated outwardly though many among them proved rebellious. Calvin calls the notion that Judah alone was then consecrated foreign to the design, since the clause about dominion merely repeats the thought; the tribe takes precedency as the most numerous, but the honour belongs equally to all. Ellicott argues from the feminine verb that the country and not the tribe is meant, and admires the art by which the divine name is withheld, a pronoun standing in its place. Wesley settles it in a line: one tribe put for all. Henry hears in the pair of words a whole constitution, sacred and civil at once, a theocracy in which what is God's sanctuary must also be his dominion. Augustine looks past the history: these things happened for examples, and the psalm predicts rather than recounts.
3:
Clarke passes on an observation of Addison's that the poet works deliberately for effect, naming no agent at all while the sea retires from the shore, the river retreats toward its source, and the hills run off like a flock of frightened sheep; only at the last is the cause suddenly introduced, and the presence of God in his grandeur solves every difficulty. Ellicott reaches the same judgment from the other end: the answer is brought in with consummate art, the mention of the power that wrought the deliverance held in suspense until the seventh verse. He also faults the received English of the third verse for weakening the picture. The word is fled, not driven back, and what is described is the descending stream turned backwards rather than parted asunder, as readers generally fancy.

Gill supplies the force of the interrogation in the fifth verse by multiplying it: what was the matter with thee, what appeared, what didst thou see, what didst thou feel, that thou shouldst flee in such haste. At the following verse he adds the one word the question needs, that the hills moved not for joy but for fear. Clarke calls the original very abrupt and the personification fine and expressive, and renders the whole passage afresh to show it.

Over the seventh verse a genuine difference of reading opens. The Hebrew has an imperative, tremble thou; but Gill notes that the imperative often stands for the past tense, and that the Syriac, Arabic, Greek and Latin all render the earth trembled or was moved. On that construction the sea, the river and the mountains are pleading their own case: is it any wonder that we fled, when the whole earth of which we are a part shook at the presence of God? Clarke agrees that almost all the versions took it so, and translates accordingly, as though the psalmist were answering his own questions. Ellicott keeps the command and presses its literal sense, be in travail. Wesley reads the past as well, remarking only that the mountains did more than was fit at the appearance of the great God.

The smaller notes fill out the scene. Ellicott observes that the verb rendered skipped is elsewhere translated dance, and that while the giving of the law was surely in the poet's thought, leaping hills belonged to every theophany. Wesley identifies them as Horeb and Sinai, two summits of a single mountain, together with their neighbours; Gill has them quaking as the glory descended. On the closing verse Gill places the miracle at two encampments, the smitten stone running in streams as if the rock itself were changed to water, and the supply following the people afterwards. Clarke ends with a philologist's flourish, translating the flint as granite, for such is the rock of Horeb, a piece of which lies before him as he writes; he judges the psalm to yield to few in the whole book for elegance and sublimity, and prints it out in an old Psalter and in Anglo-Saxon to display the affinity of the languages.
